newsitem.title: CHINA: Brewers battle to quench thirst of China drinkers.
newsitem.headline: Brewers battle to quench thirst of China drinkers.

text.p: Foreign and domestic breweries went to war this week in China's capital, seeking to quench the thirst of the world's largest potential beer market.

On a sultry summer evening, breweries from around the world set up a glitzy array of promotional stands in a scramble to seduce a thirsty crowd of some 20,000 Beijingers at the opening night on Wednesday of the Beijing International Beer Festival.

Armies of salesgirls kitted out in promotional uniforms ambushed passers-by, thrusting flags, balloons and baseball hats into their arms as rival bands blared out music ranging from country and western classics to the latest Chinese rock hits.
The largest of the stands was set up by domestic giant Yanjing Beer Group Co, China's biggest brewer, which controls 85 percent of the Beijing market.
Drinkers flocked to Yanjing, some saying price was an attraction.
Foreign breweries saw the fair as an opportunity to tout their wares.
"We just want to make ourselves known -- to raise awareness of our name and our products," said an organiser for Bass Plc's Tennents lager, produced at a joint venture plant in northeastern China.

Foreign breweries are battling to stake their claim to a share of China's army of drinkers who consumed 155 million hectolitres of beer in 1994 and are expected to drink 220 million hectolitres in 2000.

"It's a cut-throat business -- all of them are losing money," said Carl Crook, general manager of Montrose Food and Wine, a distributor of brands including Caffreys beer and the alcoholic lemon drink Hooch.
"The market will eventually catch up with supply but at the moment most foreign beer companies are budgeting a loss to stay in the market," he said.
Some breweries were moving down-market by launching cheaper alternative brands but most were still only targeting the top end of the market, he said.
And at 15 yuan ($1.80) for a beer, only Beijing's wealthier drinkers could afford to sample the ales at the 12-day fest.
"The people who drink these beers tend to be more up-and-coming well-heeled young business people," said Crook.
The average age of their target market was 20-30, he said but beer-swillers of all ages were out to savour the brews on offer at the event.
"I think it's great fun," said one mother as she gave her one-year-old son, Cao Jiawei, a sip from a can of lager.
"I don't drink beer myself but he likes a mouthful or two," she said.
